skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_app_state, get_guidelines, execute, get_screenshot, export_nodes, export_html.

Fixed — the empty result now uses the same header row as a populated one. Harness is live (200), so reload it.

**Before**
```
sql            ▸ Recent account activity · 25 rows · 14 ms      ← 12px, caret, title
sql-zero-rows    No rows matched. 0 rows · 8 ms                 ← 14px, no caret, no title
```
Three things changed at once between two states of the same tool: type scale (`text-sm` → `text-xs`), left indent (caret gone), and the title vanished in favour of a sentence.

**After**
```
sql            ▸ Recent account activity · 25 rows · 14 ms
sql-zero-rows    Executed query · No rows · 8 ms               ← same scale, same indent, same slots
                 ▸ Show query
sql-error        relation "informaton_schema.tables" does not exist
                 Executed query · No rows · 3 ms
                 ▸ Show query
```

The caret slot is *held* (an `invisible` spacer) rather than removed, so the title stays on the same left edge as every other summary line in the card — but it isn't offered as a control, because there's nothing to open. `"No rows"` replaces `"0 rows"` in the count slot, so emptiness is stated where the count already lives instead of as a separate sentence.

While in there: `total_count: 1` rendered as `"1 rows"`. Now `"1 row"`.

**Verified:** 174 tests pass, tsc clean, biome clean. New test `keeps the empty result on the same header row as a populated one` **mutation-checked** — deleting the caret spacer turns it red (`expected undefined to be '▸'`), restored and green.

result-view.collapse-matrix.test.tsx 2 +/-

export const QUERYABLE_TABLE_NAMES = new Set(QUERYABLE_SCHEMA.tables.map((t) => t.name));

/**
 * Exposed relation name → physical table, for the relations whose agent-facing
 * name differs from the engine's.
 *
 * The agent-facing product name is Behavior; `watcher` is internal engine/DB
 * vocabulary that must not reach an agent (AGENTS.md hard invariant). The
 * allowlist error enumerates {@link QUERYABLE_TABLE_NAMES} verbatim to the
 * caller, so exposing the physical names both leaked the vocabulary and told the
 * agent that `behaviors` — the name every other tool uses — does not exist.
 *
 * Foreign-key columns that point AT a behavior keep the physical name
 * (`behavior_versions.watcher_id`, `event_classifications.watcher_id`) because
 * they are the real join keys. Behavior-owned lineage columns on the
 * `behaviors` relation itself are exposed under public aliases
 * (`source_behavior_id`, `behavior_group_id`) via an explicit `expr`, so the
 * projection still reads the physical column.
 *
 * Every entry must be consumed by the CTE builder in `execute-data-sources`;
 * a relation with no physical mapping falls through to the entity-type-slug
 * branch and silently returns entities instead of erroring.
 */
const PHYSICAL_TABLE_BY_RELATION: ReadonlyMap<string, string> = new Map([
  ['behaviors', 'watchers'],
  ['behavior_versions', 'watcher_versions'],

## 2 — I was wrong about where that bug is

I said "fix the SDK to return `{error}`". I read the producer and that fix has nothing to fix: **the SDK already throws, correctly.**

`packages/server/src/utils/execute-data-sources.ts:372`
```ts
throw new Error(formatUnknownTablesError(unknown));
```
And the message it throws (`table-schema.ts:963`) literally contains:
> `This is an error, not an empty result.`

Someone already lost this argument once and fixed it at the string level.

So where did `{Tables: "<error>", ok: true}` come from? **The agent's own script caught it.** `run-script.ts:758` says the quiet part out loud — *"the guest can catch it and loop"*. The fixture confirms it:
```js
sdk_calls: 1,
sdk_call_trace: [{ path: "query", access: "read", duration_ms: 12 }],
success: true,          // ← the script's verdict, not the call's
```

The script ran `client.query`, caught the rejection, assigned the message to a key it named `Tables`, and returned `ok: true`. No renderer heuristic can fix a script that reports success for a call that failed.

**But there is a real gap, one layer down.** Look at when the trace is written (`run-script.ts:942–1012`):

```ts
appendTrace.append(sdkCallTrace, { path, orgPath, access, args, skipped: false });
return target.query(args[0] as string);      // ← appended BEFORE it runs
```
and when it rejects (`:1022`):
```ts
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ClientSdkActionError) { ...return ok:false to the guest }
  throw error;                                // ← nothing recorded, either way
}
```

**The trace is write-ahead only. Nothing on the host records that a dispatched call failed.** So `sdk_calls: 1` counts a call that errored, and the only failure signal in the whole envelope is `success`, which the guest controls. Two independent facts — *did the calls succeed* and *did the script say it succeeded* — collapse into one that reads as "everything worked."

That's the declared channel the renderer should read instead of guessing. Two ways to open it:

**A. Log it.** On rejection, host-push `{level:"warn", message:"SDK call 'query' failed: …"}`. `logs` already exists, already has that shape, the renderer already displays it (see the `failure` case). No schema change.

**B. Record it.** Add `failed`/`error` to the trace entry, so the card can say `1 SDK call · 1 failed` regardless of what the script returned.

I'd do **A now, B when something needs to branch on it.** But I'm not doing either unasked: B changes the MCP result envelope, which AGENTS.md says needs your sign-off first, and both are server-side — wrong repo for this branch. Say the word and I'll take A on a fresh branch.

## 3 — which harness cases are actually dead

Not all the T3 probes. `generic-nested-object`, `generic-array-field`, `generic-multiline-string`, `generic-long-top-string` still exercise live machinery — ValueView's per-level collapse survived the trim; only the *top-level* promotion died. Open any of them and they still differ from each other.

Three are genuinely dead, and two of them **now lie in the UI**:

```
summary-headline           "A prose summary field is promoted to the heading"
summary-two-long-strings   "…there is no basis to promote one"   (label: "(no peek)")
```
Promotion is gone and peek is gone. A reviewer reads those descriptions, looks for a heading, and finds `▸ 5 fields`. Their payloads add nothing either — an array under an arbitrary key is `generic-array-field`; long-string collapse is `generic-multiline-string`. The *only* thing that made them distinct was the tiebreak I deleted.

The third is `search-sdk`, dead by construction: the same branch removes `RICH_RESULT_MCP_META` from that tool, so a `search_sdk` result can never appear in a widget. The harness is rendering a card that will not exist.

That's a 3-case delete plus a description fix. Harness-only, same branch — say go and it's one edit.

## 4 — it *is* pushed

```
PR #812  OPEN  feat(mcp-apps): make arbitrary tool returns legible
branch   ahead 1, behind 1     ← today's amends aren't on it
```

You held it, and I've amended twice since (the T3 trim, then this header fix), so force-pushing mid-review would just churn the PR while the design is still moving. But the real blockers are structural:

- **`make ui-review` can't pass.** An Owletto pointer PR needs visual proof, and the Chrome extension isn't connected — I can't capture screenshots. No `ARTIFACT`, no pass. This is the hard one.
- **The parent PR doesn't exist yet.** The server side is sitting uncommitted in the parent worktree:
  ```
  packages/server/src/tools/mcp_app.ts       v11 → v12 resource URI
  packages/server/src/tools/registry.ts      search_sdk loses RICH_RESULT_MCP_META
  packages/server/src/__tests__/…mcp-app-resources.test.ts
  ```
  Owletto merges **last**, after the parent that carries the v12 bump. Pushing #812 to green now buys nothing.

So: not "forgot", not "blocked on you" — waiting on your design confirmation, and owing a screenshot I currently can't take.

**Confidence: high** on the run-script finding (read the write-ahead append and both rejection paths in source) and on the PR/branch state (`gh` + `git status`). **High** on which harness cases are stale — I checked each against the machinery the trim deleted, and the two descriptions are verifiably false now.

Next:
1. **Reconnect the extension** — it's the only thing standing between #812 and mergeable.
2. **A or B on the SDK trace?** A is a log line, B is an envelope field.
3. Green-light the 3-case harness delete + description fix.
4. Commit the parent server change and open the parent PR, so the pointer has something to merge behind.

## The working invocation (verified 2026-08-08)

The CLI path is NOT broken — it needs **two** overrides together. Without them
`lobu call` builds `https://lobu.ai/api/buremba/<tool>` and returns **405**;
adding only `--url` trips a credential guard ("Refusing to send stored context
credentials"). Both, plus the token pulled out of `credentials.json`:

```bash
TOK=$(python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('$HOME/.config/lobu/credentials.json'));print(d['contexts']['prod']['accessToken'])")
LOBU_API_TOKEN="$TOK" lobu call manage_operations -c prod \
  --url https://app.lobu.ai/api/v1 --raw \
  --arg action=execute --arg connection_id:=479 \
  --arg operation_key=screenshot --arg 'input:={"tab_id":<TAB>}' > shot.json
```

Note `-c` / `--url` come **after** `call` (`lobu --context` is not a flag), and
`--arg k:=<json>` for non-strings. `config.json` holds `contexts.prod.url =
https://app.lobu.ai/api/v1`; `credentials.json` holds the token separately.

**Why this matters more than the ergonomics:** a viewport PNG is ~500 KB of
base64. Through `run_sdk` (the MCP tool) that lands in the agent context —
~150k tokens per shot. Through the CLI it goes straight to a file at zero
context cost. Always use the CLI for screenshots; `run_sdk` is fine for
`evaluate` probes that return short strings.

Decode with a recursive `data_url` search (it is nested under `output`), then
`sips -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 72 -Z 1500` before embedding.

`scrollIntoView({block:"start"})` on an `h1,h2,h3,h4` whose text starts with the
section heading → `screenshot`. Scoping the selector to headings matters:
`div,section,span` matches the whole container and `block:"center"` then scrolls

`navigate` *creates* the window, so a later call cannot widen it.

## Before/after on a submodule-pointer PR

Check the submodule out at the base SHA, force a server restart, capture, restore:

```bash
git -C packages/owletto checkout --quiet <base-sha>
touch packages/server/src/server.ts   # tsx watch restarts, rebuilding vite's graph
```

`tsx watch` ignores `../owletto/**`, so touching a *server* file is what picks up
a wholesale submodule checkout. Boot took ~6 s; poll with curl, not a fixed sleep.

## 2026-08-08 (#2592): keep the image OUT of context, and pick the right machine

- **Connection 479 = `Chrome (MacBook Pro)`** is this laptop. **432 = `Chrome (Mac mini)`** is a
  *different host* and cannot reach `localhost` at all. Check
  `operations.listAvailable({connection_id}).operations[].execution_targets[].display_name`
  before capturing. `mcp__claude-in-chrome__list_connected_browsers` was still `[]`, and the
  `lobu` CLI still 405s on the malformed URL — neither is needed.
- **A shot is a ~380 KB `data_url` ≈ 95k tokens if returned.** Never let it be a tool result.
  Inside one script, feed it into an `evaluate` expression that POSTs to a local receiver —
  `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:5200/?name=x',{method:'POST',body:<JSON.stringify(dataUrl)>})` —
  and return only `post=200`. The browser runs on this machine so it reaches localhost; the
  Lobu sandbox does not. `sdk_call_trace` showing `{truncated:true,bytes:…}` confirms the
  payload never entered context. Receiver ≈ 25 lines of node, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`,
  text/plain body so it stays a CORS simple request.
- **Scratch tabs are run-scoped**: `navigate` returns `output.tab_id`, destroyed at run end, so
  a later call gets `evaluate: no tab`. Do navigate → act → screenshot in ONE script.
- **Standalone vite beats the shared `make dev`** (that server belongs to another session's
  process tree and 404s every app route after a config restart):
  `cd packages/owletto && LOBU_API_PROXY=https://app.lobu.ai bunx vite --host localhost --port 5199 --strictPort`.
  Already signed in. Org slug is **`buremba`** — hit `/` and let it redirect; a locally-seeded
  slug gives "Organization not found". Launch it with an explicit `cd` in the same command:
  shell cwd resets between calls and vite silently serves the wrong root (404s everywhere).
- ProseMirror/TipTap: focus, collapse a Range to the end, `document.execCommand('insertText',
  false, '@')`. Wait ~5 s after a tab switch — racing the mount gives `.ProseMirror` null and
  silently captures a menu-less page that looks like a real "before".
- `sips -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 68 -Z 1600` → 4 shots ≈ 474 KB → 1.21 MB artifact.

Confirmed — and your instinct is right, but the cause isn't the renderer.

**`query_ms` doesn't exist in the product.** Verified against `origin/main` across the whole parent repo:
```
$ git grep -n "query_ms" origin/main
(nothing)
```
It appears in exactly two places, both in Owletto: the harness fixture, and a renderer comment written to accommodate it.

**The fixture is fabricated.** `registry.ts:299` declares `query_sdk` with `outputSchema: SdkScriptResultSchema` — the *same envelope as `run_sdk`*: `{title?, success, return_value, duration_ms, sdk_calls, …}`. The harness instead hands it a bare `{entities, events, query_ms}`, which the real tool cannot produce.

That's the whole explanation for what you're seeing:

| | fixture shape | what renders |
|---|---|---|
| `run-sdk` | real envelope | ✓ **Completed** · 4 SDK calls · 2410 ms |
| `query-sdk` | bare object | no chrome — `isSdkResult()` is false, so `query_ms` falls through to the generic field list and gets humanized to **"Query Ms · 18"** |

So it's not a header at all. It's a payload key being rendered as a labeled field, and the status chrome is missing because the fixture never had an envelope to draw it from. On my branch the *new* `declared-query-sdk` fixture already uses the real envelope and renders `Completed · 1 SDK call · 88 ms` like everything else — the old inherited fixture is the odd one out.

Two things to fix, both real:
1. Rewrite the `query-sdk` fixture to the actual envelope, with `{entities, events}` as its `return_value`.
2. Delete the `query_ms` accommodation in the renderer (`result-view.tsx:1515` on main) — machinery built for a shape nothing emits.

**I'm not touching either yet.** `make review-fix` is still running in the worktree and has already rewritten `result-view.tsx` and both test files (176+/131−, including deleting the `search_sdk` bespoke view). Editing underneath it would collide, and none of its changes are reviewed. I'll wait for it to land, show you its diff, then fix the fixture.

content.text: The renderer passes side effects to a generic `ValueView`, so it's shape-agnostic — no prod bug there, but the harness still shows `Method/Summary` where prod shows `Path/Args`. Fixing both divergences class-wide:

input.command:

import re
p='src/mcp-apps/review/main.tsx'
s=open(p).read()
n=s.count('\n\t\t\tside_effect_preview:')
assert n==12, f"expected 12 SDK fixtures, found {n}"
assert 'skipped_calls' not in s, "skipped_calls already present somewhere"
# skipped_calls is REQUIRED in SdkScriptResultSchema; every fixture omitted it.
s=s.replace('\n\t\t\tside_effect_preview:', '\n\t\t\tskipped_calls: 0,\n\t\t\tside_effect_preview:')
assert s.count('skipped_calls: 0,')==12
# The dry-run fixture skipped exactly the one call it previews.
old='''			skipped_calls: 0,
			side_effect_preview: [
				{
					method: "events.create",
					access: "write",
					summary: "Would append one account_note event",
				},
			],
			dry_run: true,'''
assert old in s, "dry-run preview block not found"
new='''			skipped_calls: 1,

				{
					path: "events.create",
					access: "write",
					args: [{ semantic_type: "account_note", title: "Renewal follow-up" }],

s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok: 12 skipped_calls added, dry-run preview reshaped to {path, access, args}")
EOF

**Yes, `search_sdk` still exists** — the tool is untouched (`registry.ts:279`). What this branch removes is only its *widget declaration* (`mcpMeta`), so a doc lookup no longer spawns an iframe mid-reasoning. The harness case stays on purpose as a degradation guard: its own description says the shape *"must still degrade to the generic path if a result reaches the renderer."* Live check just now confirms it renders with no status line, because its payload isn't an SDK envelope — which is correct for that tool.

**The missing "ms / N calls" was the fixer damaging the product.** `make review-fix` had deleted it:

```diff
- const statusMeta = [
-   typeof value.sdk_calls === "number" ? `${value.sdk_calls} SDK call…` : null,
-   `${String(value.duration_ms ?? 0)} ms`,
+ const statusMeta = value.dry_run === true ? "dry run" : null;
- label: "SDK call trace",
```

I stopped it mid-run, backed its 1296-line patch up, and reverted. Live now:
```
run-sdk    :: Completed 3 SDK calls · 22 ms
dry-run    :: Completed 1 SDK call · 9 ms · dry run   Planned changes 1 change · not executed
query-sdk  :: Completed 1 SDK call · 18 ms  ▸ Found entities · 2 items
```

## Your "don't diverge" rule found three inventions, not one

I audited every fixture against the real handler (`sdk_run.ts:290-308`) rather than the declared schema, since the handler is what actually ships:

1. **`query_ms`** — invented key, exists nowhere in the product. It was rendering as a `Query Ms` field *and* costing the card its status line. Now the real envelope with `duration_ms: 18`.
2. **`skipped_calls` missing from all 12 SDK fixtures** — and it's *required*, not optional, in `SdkScriptResultSchema`. Added; the dry-run case gets `1`, which is what now drives its "1 change · not executed".
3. **`side_effect_preview` entries used `{method, summary}`** — real shape is `{path, access, args}`. Reshaped. The renderer passes these to a generic `ValueView`, so prod isn't broken, but the harness was showing labels the host will never send.

The fixer was right about 2 and 3 and about the `v12` bump in `check-mcp-app-bundle.mjs` (which I kept). It was wrong about deleting the status line. That's the split I acted on rather than taking or dropping its work wholesale.

One self-inflicted detour worth flagging: I ran biome with the *parent's* config from inside the submodule, which reformatted the file tabs→spaces (2497-line diff). Owletto has no biome config and uses biome's tab defaults; reformatting with those restored it to 61+/24−.

**Committed** `dbf71f09`, tree clean, 174 tests / tsc / lint green, 5 intended files.

**Confidence: high** on the fixtures now matching prod (read the handler return, not the schema — they disagree) and on the rendering (verified live in your browser, not from jsdom). **Medium** on the fixer's other ~1200 lines — I haven't reviewed them; the patch is saved at `scratchpad/codex-fixer/full.patch`.

Next:
1. **Reload 4181** (not 4179 — that's your main checkout on unmodified `main`) and confirm the status lines read right to you.
2. I should re-run `review-fix` on the settled diff, but with the statusMeta deletion pre-empted — or skip it and go straight to `make review`, since I've now reviewed its output by hand.
3. Server-side: `SdkScriptResultSchema` under-declares 5 fields the handler returns (`logs`, `duration_ms`, `sdk_calls`, `sdk_call_trace`, `sdk_call_trace_truncated`). Separate branch, and it's the same root cause as the `query_ms` invention — nothing forced fixture and schema to agree.

questions.question: A 500-row result currently puts all 500 rows in the widget DOM (32k chars). How should the widget bound it?

options.label: Paginate in place, 25/page
options.description: Add a pagination row model to DataTable. Sorting still applies across all 500 rows, so the table stays honest. Nothing dumps. Needs no Lobu link, and the widget stays self-sufficient.

options.label: Show 25, rest in Lobu
options.description: Hard cap at 25 rows with 'Showing 25 of 500 — open in Lobu'. Smallest possible widget. Caveat: sorting would only reorder the 25 shown, which misleads unless I also remove sorting when truncated.

options.label: Paginate + link out
options.description: Pagination for in-widget reading, plus an 'Open in Lobu' link on any result over one page. Most work, and the link half depends on the server change in the next question.

questions.question: "Let the user see the data in Lobu" needs a link, but query_sql / run_sdk results carry no Lobu URL today (only search_memory, save_content and get_behavior emit view_url). Adding one is an API-surface change, so it needs your sign-off.

options.label: Yes — add a result permalink
options.description: Server emits a Lobu URL on query_sql/run_sdk results (url-builder already has buildResourcePermalink). Separate branch, separate PR. This is what actually makes 'see it in Lobu' real rather than aspirational.

options.label: Not now — cap only
options.description: Bound the rendering in this branch and leave the link for later. The widget will say what it withheld but can't offer anywhere to go, so a large result is bounded but not fully answerable.

questions.question: An undeclared return with 200 keys renders all 200 as a flat field list (11k chars). Same treatment?

options.label: Cap at ~20, then a count
options.description: Show the first 20 fields and state '180 more fields'. Consistent with the tier-3 stance already taken: an undeclared bag gets stated, not exhaustively rendered.

options.label: Paginate like arrays
options.description: Reuse the 10-per-page pager that scalar arrays already use, so every key is reachable in the widget without dumping.

options.label: Leave it
options.description: 200-key returns are rare enough not to be worth the code. Only the table path gets bounded.

content.text:
Verified live: 26 `<tr>` (25 rows + header), no pager — correct, since 25 rows at page size 25 is exactly one page.

## What I changed

**`DataTable` gained pagination** (`getPaginationRowModel`, page state persisted through `viewState` like sorting already was), driven by a new `pageSize` prop. The three widget call sites plus the json-template table pass `pageSize={25}`. The web app's own `renderer.tsx` call site passes nothing and renders all rows exactly as before — I didn't change app behavior unasked.

Sorting still runs across the **whole** result and pagination applies after, so a page is a window on all 500 rows rather than a truncation of them. That distinction is why I went this way instead of slicing to 25: slicing plus a sort control would let the table claim "id ▲" while sorting only the 25 rows it happened to keep.

**Undeclared objects cap at 20 fields** with `180 more fields not shown`. Consistent with the tier-3 stance already in this branch — an undeclared bag gets stated, not exhaustively rendered.

`Pagination` moved from `result-view.tsx` into `data-table.tsx`, since a dependency can't import from its own consumer.

## Three calls I made without you

You were away, so I picked and I'm flagging each:

1. **Paginate rather than truncate** — reasoning above. Reversible if you'd rather have the harder cap.
2. **I did not add the Lobu permalink.** `query_sql` / `run_sdk` results carry no URL (only `search_memory`, `save_content`, `get_behavior` emit `view_url`), so adding one is an MCP envelope change — AGENTS.md says that needs your sign-off, and it belongs on a server branch regardless.
3. **20 fields, then a count** rather than a pager for objects.

**So half your directive is done and half isn't.** "Don't dump so much data" — done, 20× reduction, verified. "Let the user see the data in Lobu" — *not* done, because there's nowhere to send them yet. The widget now says what it withheld but can't offer a destination. That's the gap, and it's the server change in point 2.

## Also this turn

`search-sdk` is gone — you were right, and I was wrong twice before checking. `McpResultView` has exactly two consumers (the widget bundle and this harness), so a tool without `mcpMeta` has no path to it; the case was guarding an unreachable input.

**Confidence: high** on the volume fix (measured before/after with the same harness, confirmed in your browser). **Medium** on breadth — 230/230 tests pass on the surfaces I touched, but the full Owletto suite has 63 files failing on `Failed to load url @lobu/core/errors`: `packages/core/dist` isn't built in this worktree. Pre-existing and unrelated to my diff, and `pre-pr-remote` builds before checks — but I haven't proven that, so treat it as unverified until the gate runs.

Next:
1. **Reload 4181** — `?case=sql` and the generic cases; the caps only show teeth on large payloads, so the visible change is small.
2. Say the word on the **server permalink** and I'll open that branch — it's what makes "see it in Lobu" real.
3. `make pre-pr-remote` (which also settles the core-build question), then merge #812 and `ARTIFACT=… make ui-review`. The artifact needs recapturing — it predates today's changes.

content.text:
The ID is now the link. `#4939822` clicks through to `/{org}/memory?content_ids=4939822`, and the separate "Open" button is gone — one affordance, on the thing you'd click anyway. Event cards get the same treatment, with `view_url` (Lobu) and `source_url` (the external system) kept as the distinct destinations they are.

**I caught myself doing the thing you told me to stop.** I'd added `view_url` to the two event fixtures to make the link render — but no server path emits a permalink per event, so that fixture would have been tuning the card against a shape the host never sends. Reverted. Receipts keep theirs because `save_content.ts:683` genuinely emits it.

So the honest state of "IDs are links":

| | renderer | prod emits a URL |
|---|---|---|
| save_memory receipt | ✅ links | ✅ |
| search_memory profile | ✅ links | ✅ |
| **events** | ✅ ready | ❌ **server gap** |
| entities in a list | ✅ ready | ❌ |
| query_sql / run_sdk | — | ❌ |

The renderer half is done and unconditional: give it a URL and the ID becomes a link; withhold one and it stays plain text (both directions are tested). Event IDs won't actually be clickable until the server emits `view_url` — `buildResourcePermalink(slug, {kind:"event", eventId})` already exists and produces exactly the right URL, it just isn't called on that path. **That's the next branch, and it's what makes your directive real.**

A note on process: my first version of that test passed even with the link removed. The fixture was missing `created_at`/`searchable`/`indexing_status`, so `isSaveReceipt` rejected it and it rendered through the *event* path instead — testing a different component than I thought. Fixed, re-mutated, and it now fails correctly (`Unable to find an accessible element with the role "button" and name /#4939822/`).

## On "merge and test e2e"

`make pre-pr-remote` is running now. I'm not going to merge ahead of it — and two things genuinely block a merge beyond the gate:

1. **`make ui-review` needs a fresh artifact.** The one I published is from before the tier trim, the fixture corrections, pagination and the ID links. It no longer depicts the branch. Recapturing is ~6 extension runs.
2. **The parent PR doesn't exist yet.** The server commit is local. Owletto merges last, after the parent that carries the v12 bump.

**Confidence: high** on the code (232 tests, mutation-verified on the new contract, tsc and lint clean). **Unverified**: the full CI graph, and whether `packages/core` being unbuilt in this worktree hides anything — the gate settles both.

Next, in order:
1. Gate result — I'll report it when it lands.
2. Recapture the artifact against current head, publish, open the parent PR.
3. `ui-review` → merge parent → merge #812 → e2e against a real MCP host.
4. Server branch: emit `view_url` on events and query results. Without it, half of what you asked for is renderer-only.

**Refreshed UI proof: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/b5badb9a-ae23-4734-88cd-435f27526d79** — same URL, now showing current head: three before/after pairs plus four after-only cases including the save receipt with the linked ID.

## The gate caught something worth the failed run

Its staging check rejected my first attempt, and unwinding the commit to fix that surfaced **two parent-repo files still holding fixer edits I'd never reviewed** — I'd only cleaned up the Owletto side after killing codex. One of them was a real bug of mine:

```diff
  const MCP_APP_RESOURCE_ALIASES = new Map([
    ['ui://lobu/interaction/v10.html', { canonicalUri: ..., template: 'embedded' }],
+   ['ui://lobu/interaction/v11.html', { canonicalUri: ..., template: 'embedded' }],
  ]);
```

`v11` needed no alias while it *was* the canonical URI. Bumping to `v12` orphans it — and ChatGPT caches resource fetches, so any host holding a cached `v11` reference would have started 404ing after deploy. The fixer caught it; I'd have shipped it. Kept, along with its test coverage.

So the fixer's record on this branch: right about `v11`, right about `skipped_calls` and the side-effect entry shape, right about the `v12` bundle-check constant — wrong only about deleting the status line. Killing it wholesale was the wrong instinct; reviewing hunk by hunk was what saved the alias.

## Where the work stands

**Done and verified:** three-tier collapse; empty-SQL header unified; `query_ms` and the other fixture divergences corrected against the real handler; `search_sdk` case removed as unreachable; payload bounded 32k→1.6k with pagination; IDs link back to Lobu where a URL exists (mutation-verified both directions).

**Not done:** the server half — no per-event permalink, so event IDs stay plain text in prod even though the renderer is ready. And `query_sql`/`run_sdk` still carry no result URL, so a bounded large result says what it withheld without offering anywhere to go.

**Confidence: high** on the Owletto code (232 tests, mutation-checked, confirmed in your browser at 4181). **Unknown** on CI until the retry finishes.

1. Gate result → then `ARTIFACT=…b5badb9a… make ui-review`, merge parent, merge #812.
2. E2E against a real MCP host after merge — that's the only thing that exercises the actual widget binding rather than the harness.
3. Server branch for the permalinks, which is what makes "land in a Lobu URL" true rather than just supported.

Merging an Owletto PR advances `owletto/main` past the SHA that `lobu/main`
pins. `check-drift` then fails on **every open lobu PR in the repo**, not just
the one carrying the bump — it compares the pinned SHA against `owletto/main`
and cannot pass until a pointer bump lands on `lobu/main`.

Done 2026-08-05 (owletto#723 merged while its parent lobu#2509 was still
waiting on a human `/ui-approve`): six open PRs went red on a check none of
their authors could fix.

**Why:** check-drift's own rule says the pinned SHA must be reachable from
`owletto/main`, which reads like "merge owletto first". It is the opposite. The
pointer PR carries the bump, so the safe order is:

1. Get the parent lobu PR fully green **including `ui-review` approval**.
2. Merge the Owletto PR.
3. Repin to the merged SHA, push, let check-drift go green.
4. Merge the parent.

Holding the Owletto PR open scopes the red to your own PR (pinned SHA not
reachable) instead of blocking everyone.

The gate failed and I'm not merging. Here's the honest state.

## The notification lied and I nearly believed it

`bm7je34po` reported **"completed (exit code 0)"**. The log said:

```
Depot run status: failed
job integration: failed
job server-integration-vitest:matrix-2: failed
make: *** [pre-pr-remote] Error 1
```

My command was `make …; echo …; tail …` — the shell returns *tail's* status. This is the piped-exit trap, and it's the second time this session a green signal was structurally meaningless (the first being a test that passed against a mutated renderer). If I'd trusted the notification I'd have merged a red branch.

## One real failure, and it was mine

`integration` is only an aggregator mirroring the vitest matrix, so it collapses to a single test:

```
mcp-app-resources.test.ts > emits canonical null member role
  for a public-workspace reader with no membership
AssertionError: expected false to be true
```

The test drove `search_sdk` and asserted `lobu/member-role` in `_meta`. But `mcp-handler.ts:499` gates that meta on `tool?.mcpMeta?.ui` — and I removed the UI resource from `search_sdk`. **The behavior is correct; the test's vehicle became invalid.** A doc lookup with no app has no app to tell a role to.

Switched it to `render_lobu_view` (host-authored blocks, no org-private read, still declares a UI resource) so the original coverage survives. And added the assertion that was missing entirely — that a no-UI tool emits **no** role key at all, since absent and null mean different things to the host: null is an explicit downgrade, absent means unchanged. Without that test, re-adding `mcpMeta` to `search_sdk` would silently pass.

Rerunning just that lane now.

Local repro was blocked by an unbuilt worktree — `@lobu/core`, then `@lobu/connector-sdk`, then `@lobu/connector-worker`. I built the first two and root `bun run build` before giving up and using the remote lane. **That also answers the earlier open question**: the 63 Owletto test files failing on `@lobu/core/errors` were the same unbuilt-workspace condition, not my diff.

git push -q -u origin feat/mcp-app-collapse-generic-returns 2>&1 | tail -2; gh pr create --title "feat(mcp): drop the undeclared-result guesswork tier" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

The MCP result renderer had four presentation tiers. The fourth tried to make an arbitrary bag of keys look intentional — promoting a "probably the answer" field to a headline, peeking at long strings. It guessed right often enough to keep and wrong often enough to mislead, and every hour spent perfecting it made *declaring* a template less attractive.

Three tiers now: **declared**, **known shape**, **undeclared**. An undeclared return states what came back and puts the fields one click away.

Owletto: buremba/owletto#812 (pointer bumped here).

## Changes

- **Tier 4 deleted** — `readsAsSentence`, `PeekText`, `TopLevelValue`, `hasSubstance`, `HEADLINE_KEYS` (−227 net renderer lines).
- **`search_sdk` stops declaring a UI resource.** A model-facing doc lookup gives the reader nothing to verify or act on, and a declared template makes the host instantiate a widget iframe for every lookup mid-reasoning.
- **`v11` added to `MCP_APP_RESOURCE_ALIASES`.** The URI bump to `v12` would otherwise orphan it, and ChatGPT caches resource fetches — any host holding a cached `v11` reference would 404 after deploy.
- **Large payloads bounded.** `DataTable` paginates at 25 rows inside the widget (sorting still spans every row, so a page is a window on the whole result, not a truncation); undeclared objects show 20 fields then state the remainder. A 500-row result went from 501 `<tr>` / 32k chars to 26 / 1.6k.
- **Ids link back to Lobu.** `#4939822` on a save receipt is now the link to `/{org}/memory?content_ids=…`, replacing a separate "Open" button. Plain text when no url came back; both directions tested.
- **Harness fixtures corrected to the real envelope** — an invented `query_ms` key removed, required `skipped_calls` added to all 12 SDK fixtures, side-effect entries reshaped from `{method, summary}` to the real `{path, access, args}`.
- Empty/failed SQL now shares the populated result's header row instead of dropping to a looser sentence at a different type scale — which also stopped discarding the caller's `title` on exactly those two paths.

## Test evidence

`server-integration-vitest` was red on `emits canonical null member role for a public-workspace reader with no membership`:

```
AssertionError: expected false to be true
  mcp-app-resources.test.ts:622
```

Cause: the member role rides on `mcpMeta.ui` (`mcp-handler.ts:499`), and the test drove `search_sdk`, which no longer declares one. The behaviour is correct; the vehicle became invalid. Moved onto `render_lobu_view` (host-authored blocks, no org-private read, still declares a UI resource), and added the assertion that was missing entirely — a no-UI tool emits **no** role key, since absent and null mean different things to the host.

Green after the fix: `Depot run qgr02m9q61 passed`, then full `Depot run c0bhkc3326 passed`.

Renderer contracts are mutation-verified: removing the id link, the caret spacer, or the title resolver each turns the corresponding test red.
EOF

The review found **two real blockers**, both mine, and I've fixed both. Judging by the findings rather than the score (`bug_free 25` reflects two genuine defects, not noise):

**Blocker 1 — the caller's title was destructured away.**
```tsx
const { title: _title, ...body } = value;   // ← thrown out, never rendered
```
An undeclared result carrying `{title: "Quarterly summary", …}` lost its heading for every non-debug viewer. What makes this worse than a plain miss: **it's the same defect class I fixed earlier this session** on the SQL empty/error paths, and I didn't grep for other instances. "Fix the class, not the instance" — I fixed the instance. The reviewer found the one I left.

**Blocker 2 — the 20-field cap discarded the remainder.** I bounded the default correctly but left fields 21+ unreachable, and since there's no Lobu link yet, "180 more fields not shown" was a dead end. Now the first 20 render inline and the rest sit behind a `6 more fields` disclosure — default stays bounded, nothing is lost. That's the resolution to the trade-off I'd flagged when you were away; the reviewer was right that my pick lost data.

**Finding 3** — `UndeclaredResult`'s `meta` prop was dead (neither call site passed it). Removed.

Both fixes carry regression tests, and both are **mutation-verified**: making the title unrendered fails one, emptying the overflow fails the other. 234 tests green, tsc and lint clean. Full gate re-running for a fresh attestation on the new tree.

One thing worth noting about the review environment: `notes` says *"Vitest could not start because the read-only sandbox blocked its generated config file"* — so the reviewer found both defects by **SSR-probing the component directly**, not by running tests. That's why it caught what my suite didn't: my tests all went through fixtures that happened to avoid both paths.

**Confidence: high** on the two fixes (probed defects reproduced by the reviewer, now covered and mutation-checked). **Medium** on there being no third instance of the dropped-title class — I've now checked SQL, save receipts and undeclared results, but haven't exhaustively grepped every render path.

1. Gate result → then `make review` once more (the blockers were real, so a re-review is warranted, not a find-fix loop).
2. `ARTIFACT=… make ui-review` — and the artifact needs one more recapture, since the undeclared card changed again.
3. Your `/ui-approve` → merge #812 → repin → merge #2690.
4. Grep the remaining render paths for other places a caller-declared field gets destructured off and dropped.

Short answer: **the renderer is, the feature isn't, and I can't merge without you.**

## Gate status right now

Red, retrying. The failure is in a lane I didn't touch:

```
[gateway lane 1] (fail) OAuthStateStore (Postgres-backed) > (unnamed) [5000.46ms]
```

Exactly 5000ms is a timeout, in a Postgres-backed OAuth suite — my diff touches the result renderer, `mcpMeta` on one tool, the resource-alias map, and one test file. Nothing near it. It smells like flake, and attempt #2 is running, but **I'm not calling it flake until the retry says so.**

## What "fully working" means honestly

**Working and verified:** three-tier result model; empty/failed SQL sharing the populated header; large payloads bounded (32k → 1.6k, overflow reachable not discarded); titles no longer dropped on secondary paths; IDs linking back to Lobu; fixtures matching the real envelope. 234 tests, key contracts mutation-checked, confirmed in your own browser.

**Not working, by omission:** the server half you asked for. Event IDs stay plain text in prod because nothing emits a per-event permalink, and a bounded 500-row result still has nowhere to send you. The renderer is *ready* for both — it links whenever a URL arrives — but until the server emits one, "let the user see the data in Lobu" is supported, not delivered. That's a separate branch and it isn't started.

**Unverified:** no e2e against a real MCP host. The harness proves the component; it does not prove ChatGPT instantiating `ui://lobu/interaction/v12.html`. The `v11` alias fix is precisely the kind of bug only a real cached host exposes.

## When I can merge

Three things, in order:

1. **Gate green** — retry in flight, minutes away.
2. **`make review` once more** — the last pass found two real blockers, so a clean re-review is owed. Not a find-fix loop; one round.
3. **`make ui-review` + your `/ui-approve`** — and this is the actual gate. It binds human approval to the exact parent-base/pointer pair. **I cannot self-approve it**, by design. The artifact also needs one more recapture since the undeclared card changed again after the review fixes.

Then: merge #812 → repin → merge #2690. That order matters — merging Owletto first reddens `check-drift` on every open PR in the repo.

So: **1 and 2 are mine and close. 3 is yours.** Once you approve, merging is a few minutes.

**Confidence: high** on the Owletto code. **Medium** on the current gate — one unexplained lane, pending retry. **Low** on end-to-end behaviour in a real host, because nothing has tested it.

I'll report the retry the moment it lands.

skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.
